gloss_terse: duration of life, lifespan; the transient world viewed as the span of human existence
gloss_readable: The Hebrew cheled conveys the fleeting duration of mortal life, closely paralleling the Greek aion in its temporal sense. In Job 11:17 it describes a lifetime that could shine brighter than noon, while Psalm 39:5 pairs it with 'my days' in a poignant meditation on brevity. Psalm 49:1 extends the meaning toward 'world' as the collective sphere of human transience, calling all inhabitants of cheled to listen. French 'vie-ephemere' and Spanish 'mundo/duracion' together capture both the personal lifespan and the wider temporal world.

senses.1: Duration of life, lifespan, mortal span. Used in Job 11:17 and Psalm 39:5 (parallel to 'my days') to express the brevity and fleetingness of human existence. The French rendering 'vie-ephemere' aptly conveys the fragility implied. The Arabic cognate khuldun ('perpetual duration') reveals an ironic contrast: the root carries eternity, yet in Hebrew it emphasizes finitude.

gloss_terse: flint; extremely hard stone used figuratively for unyielding firmness
gloss_readable: Challamish denotes flint, the hardest common stone known to the ancient world. In Deuteronomy 8:15 God brings water from the 'rock of flint' in the wilderness, an act magnified by the material's notorious impermeability. Isaiah 50:7 applies it as a powerful simile for resolute determination: 'I set my face like flint.' Spanish 'pedernal' and English 'flint' converge on the same mineralogical image, while the German and French translations leave the Hebrew untranslated, underscoring the word's technical specificity.

senses.1: Flint, flinty rock. A stone of exceptional hardness, used literally for the rock from which God miraculously drew water in the wilderness (Deut 8:15; Ps 114:8) and for rock worked by miners (Job 28:9). In Deuteronomy 32:13 oil flows from flinty rock, hyperbolically. Isaiah 50:7 employs it figuratively for unyielding resolve, reflected consistently across Spanish 'pedernal,' English 'flint,' and the Septuagint's stereological equivalents.

gloss_terse: Helon; father of Eliab, leader of the tribe of Zebulun during the wilderness period
gloss_readable: Helon appears exclusively in Numbers as the father of Eliab, who served as the tribal leader of Zebulun during the wilderness census and march. All five occurrences cluster in the early chapters of Numbers (1:9; 2:7; 7:24, 29; 10:16), always in the patronymic formula 'Eliab son of Helon.' The Septuagint renders the name as Chailon or Chelon. The name's consistent rendering across English, Spanish ('Helon'), French ('Helon'), and German ('Helon') shows no translational variation.

senses.1: Helon, a proper masculine name. Father of Eliab, the appointed leader of the tribe of Zebulun. All five attestations appear in Numbers within census lists, tribal camp arrangements, and dedication offerings (Num 1:9; 2:7; 7:24, 29; 10:16). The Septuagint traditions (Chailon, Chelon) suggest a guttural-initial pronunciation preserved across Greek manuscript families.

gloss_terse: Helez; name of two men: one of David's mighty warriors, and a Judahite in the line of Jerahmeel
gloss_readable: Helez designates two distinct individuals in the Hebrew Bible. The first is one of David's elite thirty warriors, called 'the Paltite' in 2 Samuel 23:26 and 'the Pelonite' in 1 Chronicles 11:27, who also commanded the seventh monthly division (1 Chr 27:10). The second Helez appears in the Judahite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2:39. The BDB entry connects the name to the root meaning 'vigour.' Spanish and French renderings ('Heles'/'Helez'/'Jelets') reflect minor transliteration variation across traditions.

senses.1: Helez, a personal name meaning 'vigour.' Refers to (a) one of David's mighty warriors from the Paltite/Pelonite clan (2 Sam 23:26; 1 Chr 11:27; 27:10), and (b) a man in the Judahite genealogy descended from Jerahmeel (1 Chr 2:39). The Septuagint shows considerable variation (Sellis, Ellis, Chellis), suggesting the name's pronunciation was already fluid in the Greek transmission period.

gloss_terse: Hamutal; mother of kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah
gloss_readable: Hamutal was the wife of King Josiah and mother of two of Judah's last kings: Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. Her name possibly means 'my father-in-law is the dew,' connecting to the name Abital by parallel construction. She appears at pivotal moments in Judah's decline, named in the accession formulae of both sons (2 Kgs 23:31; 24:18; Jer 52:1). The Ketiv spelling chamital and Qere chamutal reveal an early textual variation preserved across manuscript traditions. French and German leave the Hebrew partially untransliterated, while Spanish ('Hamutal/Jamutal') reflects aspiration differences.

senses.1: Hamutal, a proper feminine name. Mother of Kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and wife of Josiah. The name's etymology is debated: the Ketiv form chamital may mean 'my father-in-law is the dew,' paralleling Abital ('my father is the dew'). All five occurrences appear in royal accession formulae (2 Kgs 23:31; 24:18; Jer 52:1), marking her political significance as mother of two of Judah's final monarchs.

gloss_terse: to dedicate, inaugurate; to train up or initiate a person or building for its intended purpose
gloss_readable: The verb chanak carries the dual sense of dedicating a building and training a person. In Deuteronomy 20:5, a man who has built a new house but not yet 'dedicated' it is exempt from battle, while Proverbs 22:6 famously urges 'train up a child in the way he should go.' The Arabic cognate reveals a vivid origin: rubbing dates on a newborn's palate to initiate nursing. Solomon's temple dedication in 1 Kings 8:63 and 2 Chronicles 7:5 shows the word at its most ceremonial. Spanish captures both senses well: 'Entrena' (train) and 'inauguraron' (inaugurated).

senses.1: To dedicate, inaugurate a structure for its intended sacred or domestic use. Applied to the dedication of Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 8:63; 2 Chr 7:5) and a newly built house (Deut 20:5). The Arabic cognate hanak ('rub the palate of a newborn') points to an initiatory root meaning: preparing something for first use. Spanish 'inauguraron' and 'dedico' reflect the ceremonial register. The related noun chanukkah ('dedication') derives from this verb, later giving the festival its name.

gloss_terse: Hosah; (1) a Levitical gatekeeper in David's time; (2) a town in the territory of Asher
gloss_readable: Hosah serves as both a personal name and a place name, deriving from the root meaning 'refuge' or 'to take shelter.' As a person, Hosah was one of the Levitical doorkeepers appointed by David for the temple service (1 Chr 16:38; 26:10, 11, 16), entrusted with guarding the western gate. As a place, Hosah appears in the boundary description of Asher's tribal allotment (Josh 19:29), though its exact location remains unidentified. The Septuagint readings vary considerably (Iasif, Sousa, Osa), suggesting early uncertainty about the toponym.

senses.1: Hosah, a proper name meaning 'refuge.' Designates (a) a Merarite Levite appointed as a gatekeeper under David, assigned to the western Shalleketh gate (1 Chr 16:38; 26:10, 11, 16), and (b) a border town in the tribal territory of Asher (Josh 19:29) whose site is unknown. The Spanish renderings 'Hosa' and French 'Chosah' preserve the aspirated initial consonant, while the divergent Septuagint forms suggest the place name was already obscure to Greek translators.

gloss_terse: wealth, treasure, stored riches; figuratively, an abundance of divine provision
gloss_readable: Chosen denotes accumulated wealth and stored treasure, used both of material riches and of God's saving provisions. Proverbs 15:6 contrasts the 'great treasure' in the righteous person's house with the trouble that plagues the wicked's income. Jeremiah 20:5 applies it concretely to the plundered wealth of Jerusalem. Most strikingly, Isaiah 33:6 transforms the concept into spiritual abundance: 'a wealth of salvations, wisdom, and knowledge.' Spanish 'riqueza' and French 'tresor' together capture the material-to-spiritual semantic arc.

senses.1: Wealth, treasure, stored riches. Refers to material abundance possessed by individuals (Prov 15:6, paired with 'great'; Prov 27:24, parallel to 'crown') or cities (Jer 20:5, the treasure of Jerusalem, alongside 'toil' and 'precious things'). Ezekiel 22:25 connects it with preciousness gained through violence. Isaiah 33:6 extends it figuratively to divine provision: 'a wealth of salvations, wisdom, and knowledge.' The Spanish 'riqueza/fortaleza' and French 'tresor' together reflect both material and metaphorical registers.

gloss_terse: Hophni; son of Eli the priest, whose corruption at Shiloh provoked divine judgment
gloss_readable: Hophni was one of Eli's two sons who served as priests at Shiloh but notoriously abused their office. Their story in 1 Samuel is one of priestly corruption met by divine judgment: they took sacrificial meat by force and treated the Lord's offering with contempt. The prophecy that both Hophni and Phinehas would die on the same day (1 Sam 2:34) was fulfilled at the battle of Aphek when the Philistines captured the ark (1 Sam 4:11, 17). The name may connect to the Sabbean hpn. All four major language traditions transliterate it consistently as Hophni/Chophni/Jofni.

senses.1: Hophni, a proper masculine name. One of Eli's two priestly sons at Shiloh, consistently paired with his brother Phinehas. All five occurrences appear in 1 Samuel 1-4, framing the narrative of priestly corruption and divine retribution: the initial mention at the Shiloh sanctuary (1:3), the death oracle (2:34), and the catastrophic fulfillment at Aphek (4:4, 11, 17). The Sabbean cognate hpn may illuminate the name's original meaning.

gloss_terse: magician, diviner-priest; member of the professional class of occult practitioners at royal courts
gloss_readable: Chartom designates the professional magicians and diviner-priests who served at ancient Near Eastern royal courts. In Daniel, they appear as one of several expert classes summoned by Babylonian kings to interpret dreams and mysteries, yet they consistently fail where Daniel, empowered by God, succeeds. The word is Aramaic in Daniel's usage and has a Hebrew cognate used of Egyptian magicians in the Joseph and Exodus narratives. Spanish 'magos,' English 'magicians,' and the consistent multilingual pattern all converge on the notion of court-based occult specialists rather than folk practitioners.

senses.1: Magician, diviner-priest attached to a royal court. In Daniel, chartom designates professional practitioners of the occult arts summoned to interpret dreams and signs alongside enchanters and sorcerers (Dan 2:10, 27; 4:7, 9; 5:11). They consistently fail to interpret divine mysteries, serving as a literary foil to Daniel's God-given wisdom. Spanish 'magos' and English 'magicians' reflect the institutional, courtly register. The related Hebrew form appears for Pharaoh's magicians in Genesis 41 and Exodus 7-9, linking Babylonian and Egyptian court magic traditions.
